claim: Cranial neural crest (CNC) cells give rise to bone, cartilage, tendons, and ligaments of the vertebrate craniofacial musculoskeletal complex.
source: Cranial neural crest (CNC) cells give rise to bone, cartilage, tendons, and ligaments of the vertebrate craniofacial musculoskeletal complex, as well as regulate mesoderm-derived craniofacial muscle development through cell-cell interactions.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by citations in the introduction (Chai and Maxson, 2006; Heude et al., 2010; Le Douarin et al., 2004).

claim: CNC cells regulate mesoderm-derived craniofacial muscle development through cell-cell interactions.
source: Cranial neural crest (CNC) cells give rise to bone, cartilage, tendons, and ligaments of the vertebrate craniofacial musculoskeletal complex, as well as regulate mesoderm-derived craniofacial muscle development through cell-cell interactions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Grimaldi et al., 2015; Han et al., 2014; Rinon et al., 2007) mentioned in the introduction.

claim: Runx2 is expressed in the CNC-derived perimysial and progenitor populations.
source: We show that Runx2, a known osteogenic regulator, is expressed in the CNC-derived perimysial and progenitor populations.
evidence: This is supported by single-cell RNA-seq data (Figure 2C-J) and immunofluorescence staining (Figure 2K-X) showing Runx2 expression in these populations.

claim: Loss of Runx2 in CNC-derivatives results in reduced expression of perimysial markers (Aldh1a2 and Hic1).
source: Loss of Runx2 in CNC-derivatives results in reduced expression of perimysial markers (Aldh1a2 and Hic1) as well as soft palate muscle defects in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization showing decreased expression of Aldh1a2 and Hic1 in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–H).

claim: Loss of Runx2 in CNC-derivatives results in soft palate muscle defects in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice.
source: Loss of Runx2 in CNC-derivatives results in reduced expression of perimysial markers (Aldh1a2 and Hic1) as well as soft palate muscle defects in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice.
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis (Figure 3G-P) showing misoriented muscle fibers, reduced muscle size, and cleft soft palate in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice.

claim: Runx2 maintains perimysial marker expression through suppressing Twist1.
source: We further reveal that Runx2 maintains perimysial marker expression through suppressing Twist1, and that myogenesis is restored in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl;Twist1fl/+ mice.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the upregulation of Twist1 in Runx2 mutants (Figure 5H-K) and the rescue of Aldh1a2 expression and muscle defects in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl;Twist1fl/+ mice (Figure 6J-R).

claim: Myogenesis is restored in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl;Twist1fl/+ mice.
source: We further reveal that Runx2 maintains perimysial marker expression through suppressing Twist1, and that myogenesis is restored in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl;Twist1fl/+ mice.
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis showing rescue of muscle fiber orientation and muscle size in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl;Twist1fl/+ mice (Figure 6B-G).

claim: Single-cell RNA-seq analysis identified 19 clusters representing 8 cell types in the developing soft palate.
source: Following integration analysis by Seurat 3, we identified 19 clusters identifiable as 8 cell types using known genetic markers: CNC-derived mesenchymal cells (Meox1+, Dlx5+), myogenic cells (Myod1+, Myf5+), neurons (Tubb3+, Stmn2+), endothelial cells (Cdh5+), erythroid cells (Hba-x+), glial cells (Plp1+, Sox10+), myeloid cells (Lyz2+), and epithelial cells (Krt14+) (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on single-cell RNA-seq data analysis and visualization in UMAP plots (Figure 1A).

claim: Eight different clusters were observed in the CNC-derived mesenchymal cell population (Clusters 0–4, 7, 8, 10).
source: Interestingly, in the CNC-derived mesenchymal cell population, we observed eight different clusters (Clusters 0–4, 7, 8, 10) (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is shown in the UMAP plot and DotPlot of signature genes (Figure 1A-B).

claim: Clusters 2 and 10 were identified as terminally differentiated osteogenic and chondrogenic cells, respectively.
source: Besides Clusters 2 and 10, which were identified as terminally differentiated osteogenic and chondrogenic cells, respectively, the cell types and functions of the other clusters in the CNC-derived mesenchymal population have not yet been well characterized.
evidence: This is based on expression of osteogenic marker Ibsp and chondrogenic marker Col2a1 (Figure 1B, E, F, M, N).

claim: Cluster 0 represents CNC-derived progenitors enriched with early CNC marker genes such as Tfap2b, Six2, and Prrx1.
source: Cluster 0 was enriched with early CNC marker genes such as Tfap2b, Six2, and Prrx1 (Simões-Costa and Bronner, 2015; Soldatov et al., 2019), so we suspected that this population might be an undifferentiated early progenitor population associated with early CNC cells, and accordingly we hypothesized that they were CNC-derived progenitors (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on gene expression analysis from single-cell RNA-seq data (Figure 1B) and supported by citations to previous studies (Simões-Costa and Bronner, 2015; Soldatov et al., 2019).

claim: Cluster 1 represents midline mesenchymal cells enriched with genes Tbx22, Wnt16, and Meis2.
source: Genes enriched in Cluster 1 (Tbx22, Wnt16, Meis2) were associated with the palatal shelf midline during development (Louw et al., 2015; Pauws et al., 2013; Warner et al., 2009; Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B); hence, we refer to this cluster as midline mesenchymal cells.
evidence: This is based on gene expression analysis from single-cell RNA-seq data (Figure 1B) and supported by citations to previous studies (Louw et al., 2015; Pauws et al., 2013; Warner et al., 2009).

claim: Clusters 3, 4, and 7 represent perimysial cells expressing genes related to head and muscle morphogenesis (Cxcl12, Igf1, Aldh1a2).
source: Clusters 3, 4, and 7 expressed high levels of genes related to head and muscle morphogenesis (Cxcl12, Igf1, Aldh1a2); we refer to them as perimysial cells (Matt et al., 2008; Schiaffino and Mammucari, 2011; Vasyutina et al., 2005; Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on gene expression analysis from single-cell RNA-seq data (Figure 1B) and supported by citations to previous studies (Matt et al., 2008; Schiaffino and Mammucari, 2011; Vasyutina et al., 2005).

claim: Cluster 8 represents mitotic cells strongly enriched in genes associated with mitosis (Top2a, Ccnb1, Ube2c).
source: Interestingly, Cluster 8 was strongly enriched in genes associated with mitosis (Top2a, Ccnb1, Ube2c) (Nielsen et al., 2020; Pines, 2011; Strauss et al., 2018) even after cell cycle regression was performed (Figure 1B). We therefore refer to this cluster as mitotic cells.
evidence: This is based on gene expression analysis from single-cell RNA-seq data (Figure 1B) and supported by citations to previous studies (Nielsen et al., 2020; Pines, 2011; Strauss et al., 2018).

claim: The Ibsp+ osteogenic cluster is mostly associated with part of the styloid process of the temporal bone in the LVP region and the pterygoid plate of the sphenoid bone in the TVP region.
source: The Ibsp+ osteogenic (Figure 1E,M) and Col2a1+ chondrogenic clusters (Figure 1F,N) were mostly associated with part of the styloid process of the temporal bone in the LVP region and the pterygoid plate of the sphenoid bone in the TVP region.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing Ibsp expression in these bone structures (Figure 1E, M).

claim: The Col2a1+ chondrogenic cluster is mostly associated with part of the styloid process of the temporal bone in the LVP region and the pterygoid plate of the sphenoid bone in the TVP region.
source: The Ibsp+ osteogenic (Figure 1E,M) and Col2a1+ chondrogenic clusters (Figure 1F,N) were mostly associated with part of the styloid process of the temporal bone in the LVP region and the pterygoid plate of the sphenoid bone in the TVP region.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing Col2a1 expression in these bone structures (Figure 1F, N).

claim: The Tfap2b+ progenitor cluster is mainly located in the lateral portions of the palatal shelves in the LVP region.
source: In the LVP region, the Tfap2b+ progenitor cluster was mainly located in the lateral portions of the palatal shelves (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing Tfap2b expression in the lateral portions of the palatal shelves (Figure 1G).

claim: The majority of the Aldh1a2+ perimysial cluster is distributed in the lateral portion while only a small portion appears in the central myogenic sites in the LVP region.
source: The majority of the Aldh1a2+ perimysial cluster was distributed in the lateral portion while only a small portion of this cluster appeared in the central myogenic sites (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing Aldh1a2 expression pattern (Figure 1H).

claim: The Hic1+ and Tbx15+ perimysial clusters are most abundantly located in the central myogenic sites of the LVP.
source: In contrast, the two other perimysial clusters (Hic1+ and Tbx15+) were most abundantly located in the central myogenic sites of the LVP (Figure 1I–J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing Hic1 and Tbx15 expression in the central myogenic sites (Figure 1I-J).

claim: Midline mesenchymal cells (Tbx22+) are mainly located in the medial portions of the palatal shelves.
source: Midline mesenchymal cells (Tbx22+) were mainly located in the medial portions of the palatal shelves (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing Tbx22 expression in the medial portions of the palatal shelves (Figure 1K).

claim: The Top2a+ mitotic cells are distributed throughout the palatal shelves and adjacent to both early progenitors and committed CNC-derived cells.
source: The Top2a+ mitotic cells were distributed throughout the palatal shelves and adjacent to both early progenitors and committed CNC-derived cells (Figure 1L).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing Top2a expression throughout the palatal shelves (Figure 1L).

claim: Perimysial markers (Aldh1a2, Hic1 and Tbx15) are expressed in the mesenchyme surrounding the tongue and masseter muscles in addition to the palatal myogenic sites of the TVP.
source: Outside of the soft palate, the perimysial markers (Aldh1a2, Hic1 and Tbx15) were expressed in the mesenchyme surrounding the tongue and masseter muscles in addition to the palatal myogenic sites of the TVP (Figure 1P–R), while near the LVP region, Hic1 and Tbx15 were also expressed in the mesenchyme surrounding the migratory path of myogenic progenitors of the LVP and the myogenic sites of the middle pharyngeal constrictor muscle and tensor tympani muscle (Figure 1I–J and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing expression of these markers in multiple muscle regions (Figure 1P-R, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-E).

claim: The perimysial lineage might be a common CNC-derived sub-population involved in the development of multiple craniofacial muscles.
source: Outside of the soft palate, the perimysial markers (Aldh1a2, Hic1 and Tbx15) were expressed in the mesenchyme surrounding the tongue and masseter muscles in addition to the palatal myogenic sites of the TVP (Figure 1P–R), while near the LVP region, Hic1 and Tbx15 were also expressed in the mesenchyme surrounding the migratory path of myogenic progenitors of the LVP and the myogenic sites of the middle pharyngeal constrictor muscle and tensor tympani muscle (Figure 1I–J and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–E). These observations suggest the perimysial lineage might be a common CNC-derived sub-population involved in the development of multiple craniofacial muscles.
evidence: This is inferred from the widespread expression of perimysial markers in multiple craniofacial muscle regions (Figure 1P-R, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-E).

claim: Tbx15 expression is absent from the hard palate.
source: Interestingly, Tbx15 expression was absent from the hard palate, but Aldh1a2 and Hic1 were expressed in the hard palate mesenchyme specifically surrounding the tooth germ (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing no Tbx15 expression in the hard palate (Figure 1—figure supplement 3F).

claim: Aldh1a2 and Hic1 are expressed in the hard palate mesenchyme specifically surrounding the tooth germ.
source: Interestingly, Tbx15 expression was absent from the hard palate, but Aldh1a2 and Hic1 were expressed in the hard palate mesenchyme specifically surrounding the tooth germ (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing Aldh1a2 and Hic1 expression surrounding the tooth germ (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D-E).

claim: Aldh1a2 and Hic1 might have different functions in the hard and soft palate.
source: Interestingly, Tbx15 expression was absent from the hard palate, but Aldh1a2 and Hic1 were expressed in the hard palate mesenchyme specifically surrounding the tooth germ (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D–F). This suggests that Aldh1a2 and Hic1 might have different functions in the hard and soft palate.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential expression patterns of these markers in hard versus soft palate (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D-F).

claim: Aldh1a2 is expressed in the medial mesenchyme of the tongue at E14.5.
source: Interestingly, we also observed that Aldh1a2 was expressed in the medial mesenchyme of the tongue, while Hic1 and Tbx15 were expressed broadly in the mesenchyme of the tongue at E14.5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,E–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing Aldh1a2 expression in the medial mesenchyme of the tongue (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).

claim: Hic1 and Tbx15 are expressed broadly in the mesenchyme of the tongue at E14.5.
source: Interestingly, we also observed that Aldh1a2 was expressed in the medial mesenchyme of the tongue, while Hic1 and Tbx15 were expressed broadly in the mesenchyme of the tongue at E14.5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,E–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing Hic1 and Tbx15 expression broadly in the tongue mesenchyme (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E-F).

claim: The expression of Aldh1a2 in the tongue gradually decreased from E12.5 to E14.5.
source: Moreover, the expression of Aldh1a2 in the tongue gradually decreased from E12.5 to E14.5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing decreasing Aldh1a2 expression over time (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-C).

claim: The Aldh1a2+ population might be specifically associated with early myogenic populations.
source: As myogenic precursors started to appear in the center of tongue primordium (Han et al., 2012), the Aldh1a2+ population might be specifically associated with early myogenic populations, while Hic1+ and Tbx15+ populations may be associated with more general myogenic populations.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal expression pattern of Aldh1a2 in the tongue and its correlation with myogenic precursor appearance (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-C).

claim: Hic1+ and Tbx15+ populations may be associated with more general myogenic populations.
source: As myogenic precursors started to appear in the center of tongue primordium (Han et al., 2012), the Aldh1a2+ population might be specifically associated with early myogenic populations, while Hic1+ and Tbx15+ populations may be associated with more general myogenic populations.
evidence: This is inferred from the broader expression pattern of Hic1 and Tbx15 in the tongue mesenchyme (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E-F).

claim: The number of CNC-derived clusters declined from seven at E13.5 to six at E14.5 and eventually five at E15.5.
source: Interestingly, we observed decreased cell heterogeneity in CNC-derived soft palate mesenchymal populations during development. The number of CNC-derived clusters declined from seven at E13.5 to six at E14.5 and eventually five at E15.5 using the same unsupervised clustering settings (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by UMAP clustering analysis at different developmental stages (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Myogenic cells formed a single cluster at E13.5 but expanded to two clusters at E15.5.
source: In contrast, myogenic cells formed a single cluster at E13.5 but expanded to two clusters at E15.5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by UMAP clustering analysis at different developmental stages (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).

claim: The number of cells in Clusters 1 (Tbx22+), 3 (Hic1+) and 4 (Tbx15+) increased from E13.5 to E15.5.
source: The number of cells in Clusters 1 (Tbx22+), 3 (Hic1+) and 4 (Tbx15+) also increased from E13.5 to E15.5, but the number of cells in CNC-derived Clusters 0 (Tfap2b+), 7 (Aldh1a2+), and 8 (Top2a+) gradually decreased.
evidence: This is shown in the bar graph of cell percentages across developmental stages (Figure 2A).

claim: The number of cells in CNC-derived Clusters 0 (Tfap2b+), 7 (Aldh1a2+), and 8 (Top2a+) gradually decreased from E13.5 to E15.5.
source: The number of cells in Clusters 1 (Tbx22+), 3 (Hic1+) and 4 (Tbx15+) also increased from E13.5 to E15.5, but the number of cells in CNC-derived Clusters 0 (Tfap2b+), 7 (Aldh1a2+), and 8 (Top2a+) gradually decreased.
evidence: This is shown in the bar graph of cell percentages across developmental stages (Figure 2A).

claim: Clusters 0, 7, and 8 may be progenitors that are transiently present at early stages of soft palate development and give rise to Clusters 1, 3, and 4.
source: The number of cells in Clusters 1 (Tbx22+), 3 (Hic1+) and 4 (Tbx15+) also increased from E13.5 to E15.5, but the number of cells in CNC-derived Clusters 0 (Tfap2b+), 7 (Aldh1a2+), and 8 (Top2a+) gradually decreased. This suggests that Clusters 0, 7, and 8 may be progenitors that are transiently present at early stages of soft palate development and give rise to Clusters 1, 3, and 4 (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal changes in cell cluster composition and supported by pseudotime analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-C).

claim: Cluster 0 is predicted to be common CNC-derived progenitors that bifurcate into two more committed groups: perimysial progenitors (Cluster 7) and another group of progenitors (a subset of Cluster 0 and Cluster 8) for midline mesenchymal cells (Cluster 1).
source: Our results predicted Cluster 0 to be common CNC-derived progenitors that bifurcate into two more committed groups: perimysial progenitors (Cluster 7) for the later perimysial population (perimysial fibroblasts) (Clusters 3 and 4), and another group of progenitors (a subset of Cluster 0 and Cluster 8) for midline mesenchymal cells (Cluster 1) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is based on pseudotime trajectory analysis using Monocle 3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-C).

claim: The fate decision between perimysial and midline mesenchymal cells happens at E13.5-E14.5.
source: The integration analysis suggested that the fate decision between perimysial and midline mesenchymal cells happens at E13.5-E14.5.
evidence: This is inferred from the pseudotime trajectory analysis showing bifurcation of cell fates during this developmental window (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-C).

claim: Top2a+ mitotic cells might be transitioning from early progenitor status to becoming more committed to a particular fate.
source: Cluster 8, predicted to be a more committed group of progenitors, represents the Top2a+ mitotic population. Because mitosis establishes a time window during which transcription factors can easily access and activate genes important for cell lineage determination (Gurdon, 2016), cells with high mitotic activity are likely undergoing cell fate transition. Therefore, those Top2a+ mitotic cells might be transitioning from early progenitor status to becoming more committed to a particular fate.
evidence: This is inferred from the known role of mitosis in cell fate determination (Gurdon, 2016) and the expression of mitotic markers in Cluster 8.

claim: Expression of Runx2 in the CNC-derived mesenchyme gradually decreased from E13.5 to E15.5.
source: Notably, we observed that expression of Runx2 in the CNC-derived mesenchyme gradually decreased from E13.5 to E15.5, suggesting it might play a role in regulating CNC-derived cell differentiation during early soft palate development (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in the UMAP plot of Runx2 expression across developmental stages (Figure 2B).

claim: Runx2 might play a role in regulating CNC-derived cell differentiation during early soft palate development.
source: Notably, we observed that expression of Runx2 in the CNC-derived mesenchyme gradually decreased from E13.5 to E15.5, suggesting it might play a role in regulating CNC-derived cell differentiation during early soft palate development (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal expression pattern of Runx2 during soft palate development (Figure 2B).

claim: Runx2 is expressed by CNC-derived common progenitors Cluster 0 (Tfap2b+), more committed progenitor cells Cluster 8 (Top2a+) and Cluster 7 (Aldh1a2+).
source: Furthermore, Runx2 was expressed not only by the CNC-derived common progenitors Cluster 0 (Tfap2b+), but also by other more committed progenitor cells, Cluster 8 (Top2a+) and Cluster 7 (Aldh1a2+), which were mainly distributed around the bifurcation regions of different lineages; only a few midline mesenchymal cells in Cluster 1 (Tbx22+) expressed Runx2 (Figure 2C–J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-expression analysis in UMAP plots showing Runx2 expression in these clusters (Figure 2C-J).

claim: Only a few midline mesenchymal cells in Cluster 1 (Tbx22+) expressed Runx2.
source: Furthermore, Runx2 was expressed not only by the CNC-derived common progenitors Cluster 0 (Tfap2b+), but also by other more committed progenitor cells, Cluster 8 (Top2a+) and Cluster 7 (Aldh1a2+), which were mainly distributed around the bifurcation regions of different lineages; only a few midline mesenchymal cells in Cluster 1 (Tbx22+) expressed Runx2 (Figure 2C–J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-expression analysis in UMAP plots showing minimal Runx2 expression in Cluster 1 (Figure 2F, J).

claim: Runx2 expression was gradually restricted from most of the palate primordium at E13.5 to only the mesenchymal cells in the putative progenitor, perimysial, and osteogenic sites in the LVP region at E14.5.
source: Runx2 expression was gradually restricted from most of the palate primordium at E13.5 to only the mesenchymal cells in the putative progenitor, perimysial, and osteogenic sites in the LVP region at E14.5; eventually, it was found only in the osteogenic regions at E15.5 (Figure 2K–M).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence staining showing the spatial restriction of Runx2 expression over time (Figure 2K-M).

claim: Runx2 was found only in the osteogenic regions at E15.5.
source: Runx2 expression was gradually restricted from most of the palate primordium at E13.5 to only the mesenchymal cells in the putative progenitor, perimysial, and osteogenic sites in the LVP region at E14.5; eventually, it was found only in the osteogenic regions at E15.5 (Figure 2K–M).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence staining showing Runx2 expression only in osteogenic regions at E15.5 (Figure 2M).

claim: There was no detectable Runx2 expression in the TVP perimysial site from E13.5 to E15.5.
source: As there was no detectable Runx2 expression in the TVP perimysial site from E13.5 to E15.5 (Figure 2N–P), we focused on the LVP region as we investigated the colocalization of Runx2 with markers of early CNC-derived progenitors and different lineages in vivo.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence staining showing no Runx2 expression in the TVP perimysial site (Figure 2N-P).

claim: Runx2 is predominantly expressed in the putative progenitor population (Tfap2b+), actively amplifying population (Top2a+) and perimysial cells (Aldh1a2+), with only a few in the midline mesenchymal cells (Tbx22+).
source: Consistent with our single-cell analysis, Runx2 was predominantly expressed in the putative progenitor population (Tfap2b+), actively amplifying population (Top2a+) and perimysial cells (Aldh1a2+), with only a few in the midline mesenchymal cells (Tbx22+) (Figure 2Q–X).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-localization analysis using RNAscope in situ hybridization and immunofluorescence (Figure 2Q-X).

claim: Runx2 may regulate differentiation of CNC-derived cells in a cell-autonomous manner at early stages, which may indirectly affect myogenesis in the soft palate mesenchyme.
source: Previous studies have shown that CNC-derived cells guide the migration and potentially regulate the maturation of mesoderm-derived myogenic precursors in the soft palate through tissue-tissue interactions (Grimaldi et al., 2015; Li et al., 2019; Sugii et al., 2017). We hypothesized that Runx2 may regulate differentiation of CNC-derived cells in a cell-autonomous manner at early stages, which may indirectly affect myogenesis in the soft palate mesenchyme.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression pattern of Runx2 in CNC-derived cells and previous knowledge about CNC-derived cell function in muscle development (Grimaldi et al., 2015; Li et al., 2019; Sugii et al., 2017).

claim: Osr2-Cre specifically labels the CNC-derived cell subset in the developing palatal mesenchyme from the beginning of palatal shelf outgrowth.
source: We first tested whether Osr2-Cre, which specifically labels the CNC-derived cell subset in the developing palatal mesenchyme from the beginning of palatal shelf outgrowth (Lan et al., 2007), could also label the CNC-derived population in the soft palate.
evidence: This is based on previous characterization of Osr2-Cre (Lan et al., 2007) and confirmed by lineage tracing in this study (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-G).

claim: tdTomato+ cells in Osr2-Cre;tdTomato mice contribute to soft palate mesenchyme including the perimysial cells surrounding all soft palatal muscles as early as E14.5.
source: We confirmed in Osr2-Cre;tdTomato mice that tdTomato+ cells indeed contribute to soft palate mesenchyme including the perimysial cells surrounding all soft palatal muscles as early as E14.5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization and immunofluorescence showing tdTomato+ cells surrounding soft palatal muscles (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-G).

claim: Co-expression of tdTomato and Runx2 in the soft palate suggests that Osr2-Cre can be used to specifically delete Runx2 in a subset of CNC-derived cells in the soft palate region.
source: Furthermore, co-expression of tdTomato and Runx2 in the soft palate suggested that we could use Osr2-Cre to specifically delete Runx2 in a subset of CNC-derived cells in the soft palate region (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–G).
evidence: This is inferred from the co-localization of tdTomato and Runx2 in the soft palate (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-G).

claim: Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice showed cleft soft palate (5/10).
source: To test whether Runx2 is a key regulator of soft palate development, we next generated Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice, which showed cleft soft palate (5/10), misoriented muscle fibers and reduced muscle size (10/10) along with defects in hard tissues including the palatine bone (3/6) and pterygoid process (6/6) (Figure 3A–F; Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by intraoral imaging and CT scans showing cleft soft palate in 5 out of 10 Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice (Figure 3A-F).

claim: Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice showed misoriented muscle fibers and reduced muscle size (10/10).
source: To test whether Runx2 is a key regulator of soft palate development, we next generated Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice, which showed cleft soft palate (5/10), misoriented muscle fibers and reduced muscle size (10/10) along with defects in hard tissues including the palatine bone (3/6) and pterygoid process (6/6) (Figure 3A–F; Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological analysis showing muscle defects in all 10 Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice examined (Figure 3G-P).

claim: Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice showed defects in hard tissues including the palatine bone (3/6) and pterygoid process (6/6).
source: To test whether Runx2 is a key regulator of soft palate development, we next generated Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice, which showed cleft soft palate (5/10), misoriented muscle fibers and reduced muscle size (10/10) along with defects in hard tissues including the palatine bone (3/6) and pterygoid process (6/6) (Figure 3A–F; Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by CT scans and histological analysis showing palatine bone and pterygoid process defects (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-J).

claim: Three out of six Runx2 mutant mice with missing palatine bones and more severe pterygoid plate defects also had soft palate clefts.
source: Notably, in analyzing the CT scans, we found that three out of six Runx2 mutant mice with missing palatine bones and more severe pterygoid plate defects also had soft palate clefts, while the other three Runx2 mutants without clefts exhibited palatine bones that were smaller, though not statistically significantly so, and less severe pterygoid plate defects, particularly shorter pterygoid plate height (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–J), suggesting the severity of skeletal defects is associated with the variability of soft palate clefts in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice.
evidence: This is based on analysis of CT scans from 6 Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-J).

claim: The severity of skeletal defects is associated with the variability of soft palate clefts in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice.
source: Notably, in analyzing the CT scans, we found that three out of six Runx2 mutant mice with missing palatine bones and more severe pterygoid plate defects also had soft palate clefts, while the other three Runx2 mutants without clefts exhibited palatine bones that were smaller, though not statistically significantly so, and less severe pterygoid plate defects, particularly shorter pterygoid plate height (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–J), suggesting the severity of skeletal defects is associated with the variability of soft palate clefts in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between skeletal defect severity and cleft palate penetrance in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-J).

claim: The height of pterygoid plate was reduced in the TVP region of Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice.
source: Consistent with the CT scans, histological analysis showed that the height of pterygoid plate was reduced and muscle attachment was abnormal in the TVP region of Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice (Figure 3G–H,L–M).
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological analysis showing reduced pterygoid plate height (Figure 3G-H, L-M).

claim: Muscle attachment was abnormal in the TVP region of Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice.
source: Consistent with the CT scans, histological analysis showed that the height of pterygoid plate was reduced and muscle attachment was abnormal in the TVP region of Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice (Figure 3G–H,L–M).
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological analysis showing abnormal muscle attachment (Figure 3G-H, L-M).

claim: The tendon tissue did not extend to the midline in the palate primordium in the TVP region in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice at E16.5.
source: Because the aponeurosis serves the important function of attaching the hard tissue to the muscle, we also analyzed the fibrous tendon tissue marked by Scx by RNAscope in situ hybridization. The tendon tissue did not extend to the midline in the palate primordium in the TVP region in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice as it did in the controls at E16.5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3I–L).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing altered Scx expression pattern (Figure 3—figure supplement 3I-L).

claim: The aponeurosis in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice was thinner and did not stretch from the lateral-oral side to the medial-nasal side at P0.
source: It could be seen more clearly at P0 that the aponeurosis in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice was thinner and it did not stretch from the lateral-oral side to the medial-nasal side as it did in control mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A–D), suggesting its attachment to the posterior bone probably was likely abnormal.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing altered aponeurosis structure (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A-D).

claim: The muscle attachment defect of the TVP might be due to disruption of the hard tissue and aponeurosis.
source: As Runx2 is not expressed in the perimysial site of the TVP region, Therefore, this muscle attachment defect of the TVP might be due to disruption of the hard tissue and aponeurosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of Runx2 expression in the TVP perimysial site and the observed defects in hard tissue and aponeurosis (Figure 2N-P, Figure 3—figure supplement 3I-L, Figure 3—figure supplement 4A-D).

claim: The muscles were reduced in size in the LVP region in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice compared to controls.
source: In the LVP region, the muscles were reduced in size in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice compared to controls (Figure 3I–K,N–P).
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological analysis showing reduced muscle size (Figure 3I-K, N-P).

claim: A significant number of LVP muscle fibers had anterior-posterior alignment in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice, compared to the uniform lateral-medial alignment of LVP muscle fibers in controls.
source: Interestingly, a significant number of LVP muscle fibers had anterior-posterior alignment in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice (Figure 3O–P), compared to the uniform lateral-medial alignment of LVP muscle fibers in controls (Figure 3J–K).
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological analysis showing misoriented muscle fibers (Figure 3J-K, O-P).

claim: The muscle fibers were mis-oriented in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice, similar to the phenotype seen in patients with cleft soft palate.
source: Interestingly, a significant number of LVP muscle fibers had anterior-posterior alignment in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice (Figure 3O–P), compared to the uniform lateral-medial alignment of LVP muscle fibers in controls (Figure 3J–K). This suggests that the muscle fibers were mis-oriented, similar to the phenotype seen in patients with cleft soft palate.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of muscle fiber orientation in mutant mice to the known phenotype in cleft palate patients (Figure 3J-K, O-P).

claim: The muscle fibers had centralized nuclei in the soft palate of Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice, which suggests that they had muscle differentiation defects.
source: Additionally, we observed that the muscle fibers had centralized nuclei in the soft palate of Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice, which suggests that they had muscle differentiation defects (Figure 3P).
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological analysis showing centralized nuclei in muscle fibers (Figure 3P).

claim: Similar muscle defects were also observed in other palatal muscles such as the PLP.
source: Similar muscle defects were also observed in other palatal muscles such as the PLP (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C–D,G–H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological analysis showing muscle defects in the PLP region (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C-D, G-H).

claim: Loss of Runx2 leads directly to defects in CNC-derived cells and indirectly to muscle defects in the soft palate.
source: We concluded that loss of Runx2 leads directly to defects in CNC-derived cells and indirectly to muscle defects in the soft palate.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed defects in CNC-derived tissues and muscles in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice (Figure 3).

claim: There was no apparent change of early myogenic marker MyoD expression between control and Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice at E13.5 in the LVP.
source: In the LVP, there was no apparent change of early myogenic marker MyoD expression between control and Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice at E13.5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence staining showing similar MyoD expression at E13.5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B).

claim: MyoD staining revealed that defects started to appear at E14.5 in the LVP.
source: MyoD staining revealed that defects started to appear at E14.5 (Figure 4A–B), when the palatal shelves began to grow and protrude towards the midline.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence staining showing altered MyoD expression at E14.5 (Figure 4A-B).

claim: Expression of the late myogenic marker MHC was decreased in the soft palate of Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice compared to controls at E15.5.
source: Expression of the late myogenic marker MHC was decreased in the soft palate of Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice compared to controls at E15.5 (Figure 4C–D), suggesting delayed muscle differentiation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence staining showing reduced MHC expression at E15.5 (Figure 4C-D).

claim: The reduced expression of MHC suggests delayed muscle differentiation in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice.
source: Expression of the late myogenic marker MHC was decreased in the soft palate of Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice compared to controls at E15.5 (Figure 4C–D), suggesting delayed muscle differentiation.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced expression of the late myogenic marker MHC (Figure 4C-D).

claim: The reduced expression of MHC persisted in the soft palate of Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice at E16.5.
source: This reduced expression of MHC persisted in the soft palate of Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice at E16.5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence staining showing continued reduced MHC expression at E16.5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D).

claim: More immature myoblasts and fewer differentiated myofibers were present in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice at E15.5.
source: MHC staining suggested that the myoblasts had fused to form myofibers, which were uniformly aligned in layers running in the lateral-to-medial direction in the LVP of control samples at E15.5 (Figure 4C). However, more immature myoblasts and fewer differentiated myofibers were present in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice (Figure 4D) and the myofibers extended in different directions, potentially hindering further muscle development and compromising physiological function.
evidence: This is demonstrated by MHC immunofluorescence staining showing altered muscle differentiation (Figure 4C-D).

claim: The myofibers extended in different directions in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice, potentially hindering further muscle development and compromising physiological function.
source: MHC staining suggested that the myoblasts had fused to form myofibers, which were uniformly aligned in layers running in the lateral-to-medial direction in the LVP of control samples at E15.5 (Figure 4C). However, more immature myoblasts and fewer differentiated myofibers were present in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice (Figure 4D) and the myofibers extended in different directions, potentially hindering further muscle development and compromising physiological function.
evidence: This is demonstrated by MHC immunofluorescence staining showing misoriented myofibers (Figure 4D).

claim: The proliferation rate of MyoD- CNC-derived cells did not have significant difference in the perimysial sites of Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice compared to controls at E14.5 and E15.5.
source: In the LVP region at E14.5 and E15.5, the proliferation rate of MyoD- CNC-derived cells did not have significant difference in the perimysial sites of Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice compared to controls (Figure 4E–H,I,K).
evidence: This is demonstrated by BrdU incorporation assay showing no significant difference in CNC-derived cell proliferation (Figure 4E-H, I, K).

claim: The proliferation rate of MyoD+ myogenic cells was not significantly different between controls and Runx2 mutants at E14.5.
source: The proliferation rate of MyoD+ myogenic cells was not significantly different between controls and Runx2 mutants at E14.5 (Figure 4E–F,J), but a significant reduction in the proliferation rate was observed in Runx2 mutants at E15.5 (Figure 4G–H,L).
evidence: This is demonstrated by BrdU incorporation assay showing no significant difference in myogenic cell proliferation at E14.5 (Figure 4E-F, J).

claim: A significant reduction in the proliferation rate of MyoD+ myogenic cells was observed in Runx2 mutants at E15.5.
source: The proliferation rate of MyoD+ myogenic cells was not significantly different between controls and Runx2 mutants at E14.5 (Figure 4E–F,J), but a significant reduction in the proliferation rate was observed in Runx2 mutants at E15.5 (Figure 4G–H,L).
evidence: This is demonstrated by BrdU incorporation assay showing significantly reduced myogenic cell proliferation at E15.5 (Figure 4G-H, L).

claim: The number of apoptotic cells was indistinguishable between controls and mutants at E14.5 and E15.5.
source: We also performed caspase3 immunofluorescence staining to investigate cell apoptosis. The number of apoptotic cells was indistinguishable between controls and mutants at E14.5 and E15.5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by caspase3 immunofluorescence staining showing no significant difference in apoptosis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E-H).

claim: Altered signaling in CNC-derived cells might cause the reduction of MyoD expression as well as proliferation defects of myogenic cells in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice.
source: It is worth noting that although the proliferation rate of CNC-derived cells in the Runx2 mutant mice were not significantly different from that of the controls, we observed that they had fewer and less proliferative MyoD+ cells than Runx2fl/fl control mice. These differences might be due to altered signaling in CNC-derived cells causing the reduction of MyoD expression as well as proliferation defects of myogenic cells in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed reduction in MyoD+ cells and their proliferation despite normal CNC-derived cell proliferation (Figure 4E-H, I-L).

claim: The composition of the CNC-derived cells was altered in the Runx2 mutants compared to controls at E14.5.
source: Using integration analysis based on shared variance, we identified similar cell clusters in the soft palates of control and Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice at this stage. However, the composition of the CNC-derived cells was altered in the Runx2 mutants compared to controls (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by integration analysis of single-cell RNA-seq data showing altered cell cluster composition (Figure 5A).

claim: The percentage of perimysial cells (Cluster 4) in the population decreased in Runx2 mutants.
source: Using markers of different subtypes of CNC-derived cells, we observed that the percentage of perimysial cells (Cluster 4) in the population decreased in Runx2 mutants, while the percentage of midline mesenchymal cells (Clusters 0 and 3) increased (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in the bar graph comparing cell percentages between control and mutant (Figure 5B).

claim: The percentage of midline mesenchymal cells (Clusters 0 and 3) increased in Runx2 mutants.
source: Using markers of different subtypes of CNC-derived cells, we observed that the percentage of perimysial cells (Cluster 4) in the population decreased in Runx2 mutants, while the percentage of midline mesenchymal cells (Clusters 0 and 3) increased (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in the bar graph comparing cell percentages between control and mutant (Figure 5B).

claim: In situ RNAscope staining revealed decreased expression of perimysial markers in the soft palates of Runx2 mutants compared to controls at E14.5.
source: Moreover, in situ RNAscope staining revealed decreased expression of perimysial markers in the soft palates of Runx2 mutants compared to controls at E14.5, suggesting the CNC-derived perimysial populations were affected, potentially leading to further myogenic defects (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing reduced expression of Hic1 and Aldh1a2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-H).

claim: The CNC-derived perimysial populations were affected in Runx2 mutants, potentially leading to further myogenic defects.
source: Moreover, in situ RNAscope staining revealed decreased expression of perimysial markers in the soft palates of Runx2 mutants compared to controls at E14.5, suggesting the CNC-derived perimysial populations were affected, potentially leading to further myogenic defects (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–H).
evidence: This is inferred from the decreased expression of perimysial markers and the known role of perimysial cells in muscle development (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-H).

claim: Bulk RNA-seq identified that certain genes associated with specific types of CNC-derived cells were differentially expressed in the Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice.
source: Consistent with the scRNA-seq results, bulk RNA-seq also identified that certain genes associated with specific types of CNC-derived cells were differentially expressed in the Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by bulk RNA-seq analysis showing differential gene expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I).

claim: A number of genes not exclusively associated with specific types of CNC-derived cells, including Twist1 and Meox2, were also identified as being differentially expressed in the bulk RNA-seq analysis.
source: A number of genes not exclusively associated with specific types of CNC-derived cells, including Twist1 and Meox2, were also identified as being differentially expressed in the bulk RNA-seq analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by bulk RNA-seq analysis showing differential expression of Twist1 and Meox2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I).

claim: Twist1 inhibits binding of Runx2 to its downstream targets and antagonizes Runx2's function in osteoblasts.
source: We focused our attention on Twist1, which inhibits binding of Runx2 to its downstream targets and antagonizes Runx2's function in osteoblasts (Bialek et al., 2004).
evidence: This is based on previous studies showing the antagonistic interaction between Twist1 and Runx2 (Bialek et al., 2004).

claim: Twist1 is primarily expressed in midline mesenchymal cells (Tbx22+), while its expression in CNC-derived common progenitors and perimysial cells (Tfap2b+; Aldh1a2+) is relatively low.
source: Based on the integration analysis of E13.5-E15.5 single-cell transcriptomes from controls, we observed Twist1 was primarily expressed in midline mesenchymal cells (Tbx22+), while its expression in CNC-derived common progenitors and perimysial cells (Tfap2b+; Aldh1a2+) was relatively low (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-expression analysis in UMAP plots showing Twist1 expression pattern (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).

claim: At E13.5, Twist1 is expressed at a low level in the palate primordium and perimysial sites in the LVP region.
source: In the LVP region, at E13.5 Twist1 was expressed at a low level in the palate primordium and perimysial sites (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing low Twist1 expression at E13.5 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B-C).

claim: At E14.5, expression of Twist1 in the palate primordium had increased, whereas its expression was maintained at a low level in the perimysial site.
source: At E14.5, expression of Twist1 in the palate primordium had increased, whereas its expression was maintained at a low level in the perimysial site (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing increased Twist1 expression in the palate primordium but low expression in the perimysial site at E14.5 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D-E).

claim: At E15.5, Twist1 showed a similar expression pattern to that of E14.5.
source: At E15.5, Twist1 showed a similar expression pattern to that of E14.5 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F–G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing similar Twist1 expression pattern at E15.5 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F-G).

claim: The spatiotemporally specific Twist1 expression in the palate primordium and myogenic regions of the soft palate is accompanied by an opposite trend in Runx2 expression in the same regions at the same stages.
source: This spatiotemporally specific Twist1 expression in the palate primordium and myogenic regions of the soft palate was accompanied by an opposite trend in Runx2 expression in the same regions at the same stages.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing Twist1 and Runx2 expression patterns across developmental stages (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B-G, Figure 2K-M).

claim: Expression levels of Runx2 and Twist1 are tightly coordinated during soft palate development.
source: This spatiotemporally specific Twist1 expression in the palate primordium and myogenic regions of the soft palate was accompanied by an opposite trend in Runx2 expression in the same regions at the same stages. This is perhaps shown most clearly by the colocalization of Runx2 and Twist1 in the LVP region at E14.5 (Figure 5D–G), which suggested that expression levels of Runx2 and Twist1 are tightly coordinated during soft palate development.
evidence: This is inferred from the complementary expression patterns of Runx2 and Twist1 (Figure 5D-G).

claim: Expression of Twist1 is upregulated in most of the palatal shelf region including the perimysial cells in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice.
source: Interestingly, we discovered that expression of Twist1 was upregulated in most of the palatal shelf region including the perimysial cells in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice (Figure 5H–K), which suggests that upregulation of Twist1 in the CNC-derived cells may interrupt their fate determination.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing increased Twist1 expression in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice (Figure 5H-K).

claim: Upregulation of Twist1 in the CNC-derived cells may interrupt their fate determination.
source: Interestingly, we discovered that expression of Twist1 was upregulated in most of the palatal shelf region including the perimysial cells in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice (Figure 5H–K), which suggests that upregulation of Twist1 in the CNC-derived cells may interrupt their fate determination.
evidence: This is inferred from the upregulation of Twist1 in Runx2 mutants and the altered cell fate composition (Figure 5H-K, Figure 5A-B).

claim: Both Runx2 and Twist1 binding sites are present in the regulatory region located around 15–40 kb downstream of the genetic locus of perimysial marker Aldh1a2.
source: Based on the complimentary expression patterns of Runx2 and Twist1 in the soft palate, we hypothesized that they may oppose each other in regulating their common downstream targets which are important for fate determination of CNC-derived cells. Therefore, we performed ATAC-seq and found that both Runx2 and Twist1 binding sites are present in the regulatory region located around 15–40 kb downstream of the genetic locus of perimysial marker Aldh1a2 (Figure 6A), suggesting that both Runx2 and Twist1 might directly regulate the expression of Aldh1a2.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ATAC-seq analysis showing Runx2 and Twist1 binding sites near Aldh1a2 (Figure 6A).

claim: Both Runx2 and Twist1 might directly regulate the expression of Aldh1a2.
source: Based on the complimentary expression patterns of Runx2 and Twist1 in the soft palate, we hypothesized that they may oppose each other in regulating their common downstream targets which are important for fate determination of CNC-derived cells. Therefore, we performed ATAC-seq and found that both Runx2 and Twist1 binding sites are present in the regulatory region located around 15–40 kb downstream of the genetic locus of perimysial marker Aldh1a2 (Figure 6A), suggesting that both Runx2 and Twist1 might directly regulate the expression of Aldh1a2.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of Runx2 and Twist1 binding sites in the regulatory region of Aldh1a2 (Figure 6A).

claim: Runx2 and Twist1 are likely to regulate Aldh1a2 independently because their binding sites are more than 20 kb apart.
source: However, as the binding sites of those two transcription factors are more than 20 kb apart, they are likely to regulate Aldh1a2 independently.
evidence: This is inferred from the distance between Runx2 and Twist1 binding sites in the Aldh1a2 regulatory region (Figure 6A).

claim: None of the five newborn Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl;Twist1fl/+ pups had palatal clefts, compared to the 50% penetrance of cleft soft palate in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice.
source: Histological analysis confirmed that the palatal stromal mesenchyme, pterygoid plate, and muscle defects were all indeed rescued in these mice. None of the five newborn Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl;Twist1fl/+ pups we collected had palatal clefts, compared to the 50% penetrance of cleft soft palate in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice (Figure 6B–G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological analysis showing no cleft palate in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl;Twist1fl/+ mice (Figure 6B-G).

claim: Pterygoid plate height was restored in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl;Twist1fl/+ mice.
source: Pterygoid plate height was restored in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl;Twist1fl/+ mice (Figure 6B–D,H), and muscle fiber orientation and muscle size were also recovered (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological analysis and quantification showing restored pterygoid plate height (Figure 6B-D, H).

claim: Muscle fiber orientation and muscle size were recovered in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl;Twist1fl/+ mice.
source: Pterygoid plate height was restored in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl;Twist1fl/+ mice (Figure 6B–D,H), and muscle fiber orientation and muscle size were also recovered (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological analysis showing recovered muscle fiber orientation and size (Figure 6E-G).

claim: Aldh1a2 was downregulated in the region where Runx2 was deleted in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice at E14.5.
source: Aldh1a2 was downregulated in the region (Figure 6K) where Runx2 was deleted (Figure 6N) and Twist1 expression was expanded in the soft palate of Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice (Figure 6Q).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing reduced Aldh1a2 expression in Runx2 mutants (Figure 6K).

claim: Twist1 expression was expanded in the soft palate of Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice at E14.5.
source: Aldh1a2 was downregulated in the region (Figure 6K) where Runx2 was deleted (Figure 6N) and Twist1 expression was expanded in the soft palate of Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice (Figure 6Q).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing expanded Twist1 expression in Runx2 mutants (Figure 6Q).

claim: The expression of Aldh1a2 was restored in the Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl;Twist1fl/+ mice at E14.5.
source: Compared to Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice, the expression of Aldh1a2 was restored in the Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl;Twist1fl/+mice at E14.5 (Figure 6L).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing restored Aldh1a2 expression in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl;Twist1fl/+ mice (Figure 6L).

claim: Runx2 and Twist1 exhibit opposite regulatory effects on the expression of Aldh1a2 in a subset of CNC-derived cells, which may be important for regulating muscle differentiation in the soft palate.
source: Compared to Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice, the expression of Aldh1a2 was restored in the Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl;Twist1fl/+mice at E14.5 (Figure 6L). This suggests that Runx2 and Twist1 exhibit opposite regulatory effects on the expression of Aldh1a2 in a subset of CNC-derived cells, which may be important for regulating muscle differentiation in the soft palate.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue of Aldh1a2 expression and muscle defects by Twist1 haploinsufficiency (Figure 6L, Figure 6B-G).

claim: Runx2 activates the expression of Aldh1a2 through repressing Twist1 instead of directly activating Aldh1a2 during normal soft palate muscle development.
source: Since haploinsufficiency of Twist1 in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl;Twist1fl/+ mice rescues the expression of Aldh1a, it is most likely that Runx2 activates the expression of Aldh1a2 through repressing Twist1 instead of directly activating Aldh1a2 during normal soft palate muscle development (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic rescue experiment showing that reducing Twist1 levels restores Aldh1a2 expression in Runx2 mutants (Figure 6L, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

claim: Aldh1a2 is an important enzyme for retinoic acid signaling, which is crucial for neural crest cells as they guide the positioning of extraocular muscles.
source: Consistent with our findings, Aldh1a2 is known as an important enzyme for retinoic acid signaling, which is crucial for neural crest cells as they guide the positioning of extraocular muscles (Matt et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on previous studies showing the role of Aldh1a2 in retinoic acid signaling and muscle development (Matt et al., 2008).

claim: The Hic1+ population represents a source of quiescent mesenchymal progenitors that play important roles during the regeneration of skeletal muscles in the limbs.
source: The potential myogenic-supportive function of Hic1 has been confirmed by the recent finding that the Hic1+ population represents a source of quiescent mesenchymal progenitors that play important roles during the regeneration of skeletal muscles in the limbs (Scott et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on a recent study showing the role of Hic1+ cells in muscle regeneration (Scott et al., 2019).

claim: Aldh1a2 and Hic1 might be novel markers for CNC-derived perimysial tissues, which may perform important pro-myogenic functions during muscle development.
source: Consistent with our findings, Aldh1a2 is known as an important enzyme for retinoic acid signaling, which is crucial for neural crest cells as they guide the positioning of extraocular muscles (Matt et al., 2008). The potential myogenic-supportive function of Hic1 has been confirmed by the recent finding that the Hic1+ population represents a source of quiescent mesenchymal progenitors that play important roles during the regeneration of skeletal muscles in the limbs (Scott et al., 2019). Hence, Aldh1a2 and Hic1 might be novel markers for CNC-derived perimysial tissues, which may perform important pro-myogenic functions during muscle development.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression pattern of Aldh1a2 and Hic1 in perimysial tissues and their known roles in muscle development (Matt et al., 2008; Scott et al., 2019).

claim: The least differentiated Tfap2b+ subpopulation is located in the lateral region of the soft palate during the early stages of its development.
source: During embryonic development, the palatal shelves grow in a lateral-to-medial direction both before and after their elevation (Bush and Jiang, 2012). Consistent with this, our in vivo analysis shows that the least differentiated Tfap2b+ subpopulation is located in the lateral region of the soft palate during the early stages of its development, and the perimysial and midline mesenchymal populations reside in central myogenic sites and the medial region of the soft palate.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing Tfap2b expression in the lateral region (Figure 1G).

claim: The perimysial and midline mesenchymal populations reside in central myogenic sites and the medial region of the soft palate.
source: During embryonic development, the palatal shelves grow in a lateral-to-medial direction both before and after their elevation (Bush and Jiang, 2012). Consistent with this, our in vivo analysis shows that the least differentiated Tfap2b+ subpopulation is located in the lateral region of the soft palate during the early stages of its development, and the perimysial and midline mesenchymal populations reside in central myogenic sites and the medial region of the soft palate.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing perimysial markers in central myogenic sites and Tbx22 in the medial region (Figure 1H-K).

claim: Several transcription factors regulate the development of different components of a musculoskeletal complex in a coordinated fashion to form a functional unit.
source: Recently, studies have found that several transcription factors regulate the development of different components of a musculoskeletal complex in a coordinated fashion to form a functional unit (Colasanto et al., 2016; Hasson et al., 2010; Mathew et al., 2011; Vickerman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on previous studies showing coordinated regulation of musculoskeletal development (Colasanto et al., 2016; Hasson et al., 2010; Mathew et al., 2011; Vickerman et al., 2011).

claim: Loss of Runx2 in CNC-derived cells of the soft palate mesenchyme leads to multiple tissue defects in the soft palate, including fibrous tendon tissue, soft palate cleft and muscle defects.
source: Our study shows that Runx2 is expressed in CNC-derived cells involved in early cell fate determination and in perimysial cells in the soft palate mesenchyme. Loss of Runx2 in CNC-derived cells of the soft palate mesenchyme leads to multiple tissue defects in the soft palate, including fibrous tendon tissue, soft palate cleft and muscle defects.
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological analysis and CT scans showing multiple tissue defects in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl mice (Figure 3).

claim: There is a fate change of CNC-derived cells from perimysial cells to midline mesenchymal cells in the soft palate of Runx2 mutant mice.
source: There is a fate change of CNC-derived cells from perimysial cells to midline mesenchymal cells in the soft palate of Runx2 mutant mice.
evidence: This is demonstrated by single-cell RNA-seq analysis showing altered cell cluster composition in Runx2 mutants (Figure 5A-B).

claim: Loss of Runx2 affecting perimysial cell differentiation may in turn affect their secretion of signaling cues that promote muscle proliferation and differentiation.
source: As perimysial cells are closely associated with muscle development, loss of Runx2 affecting their differentiation may in turn affect their secretion of signaling cues that promote muscle proliferation and differentiation.
evidence: This is inferred from the altered perimysial cell fate and the known role of perimysial cells in muscle development.

claim: Multiple genes associated with pro-myogenic secreted factors specifically expressed by perimysial populations, such as Aldh1a2, Igf1, Cxcl12, and Cthrc1, are downregulated in Runx2 mutant mice.
source: Indeed, we show that multiple genes associated with pro-myogenic secreted factors specifically expressed by perimysial populations, such as Aldh1a2, Igf1, Cxcl12, and Cthrc1, are downregulated in Runx2 mutant mice (Matt et al., 2008; Schiaffino and Mammucari, 2011; Spector et al., 2013; Vasyutina et al., 2005).
evidence: This is demonstrated by bulk RNA-seq analysis showing downregulation of these genes in Runx2 mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I).

claim: Runx2 regulates the differentiation of CNC-derived cells during early tooth and intramembranous bone formation through distinct sets of downstream targets.
source: Transcription factors often regulate different downstream targets in distinct tissues. Previous studies have shown that Runx2 regulates the differentiation of CNC-derived cells during early tooth and intramembranous bone formation through distinct sets of downstream targets including Gli1, Lef1, Tcf1, Wnt10a, Wnt10b, and Tgfb1 in osteogenic cells and Dusp6, Enpp1, Igfbp3, and Fgf3 in dental mesenchyme (James et al., 2006).
evidence: This is based on previous studies showing tissue-specific Runx2 targets (James et al., 2006).

claim: Downstream targets of Runx2 have differing responses to the loss of Runx2 in the soft tissue.
source: In this study, we have shown that downstream targets of Runx2 have differing responses to the loss of Runx2 in the soft tissue. Perimysial markers were specifically downregulated upon loss of Runx2, while genes expressed specifically in the midline mesenchymal cells and a set of more broadly expressed genes are upregulated.
evidence: This is demonstrated by bulk RNA-seq and in situ hybridization showing differential gene expression changes in Runx2 mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: Perimysial markers were specifically downregulated upon loss of Runx2.
source: In this study, we have shown that downstream targets of Runx2 have differing responses to the loss of Runx2 in the soft tissue. Perimysial markers were specifically downregulated upon loss of Runx2, while genes expressed specifically in the midline mesenchymal cells and a set of more broadly expressed genes are upregulated.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization showing reduced expression of Aldh1a2 and Hic1 in Runx2 mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-H).

claim: Genes expressed specifically in the midline mesenchymal cells and a set of more broadly expressed genes are upregulated upon loss of Runx2.
source: In this study, we have shown that downstream targets of Runx2 have differing responses to the loss of Runx2 in the soft tissue. Perimysial markers were specifically downregulated upon loss of Runx2, while genes expressed specifically in the midline mesenchymal cells and a set of more broadly expressed genes are upregulated.
evidence: This is demonstrated by bulk RNA-seq showing upregulation of midline mesenchymal markers and general markers in Runx2 mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I).

claim: Runx2's different regulatory effects on distinct downstream targets in the soft palate mesenchyme could be direct or indirect.
source: Although Runx2 has both transcriptional activation and repression domains, its different regulatory effects on distinct downstream targets in the soft palate mesenchyme could be direct or indirect.
evidence: This is inferred from the known dual function of Runx2 as both activator and repressor.

claim: Loss of Runx2 in CNC-derived cells leads to abnormal upregulation of Twist1 in the perimysial population.
source: In this study, we reveal complimentary expression patterns of Runx2 and Twist1 in the perimysial and midline mesenchymal populations during soft palate development, which seems to confirm their antagonistic interaction (Bialek et al., 2004). However, in contrast to the previously reported model of Twist1 and Runx2 antagonistic interaction, we show that loss of Runx2 in CNC-derived cells leads to abnormal upregulation of Twist1 in the perimysial population.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAscope in situ hybridization showing increased Twist1 expression in the perimysial region of Runx2 mutants (Figure 5H-K).

claim: Suppression of Twist1 in the perimysial population by Runx2 is necessary to maintain the expression level of perimysial marker gene Aldh1a2, which may be important for regulating muscle development.
source: Further analysis has shown that suppression of Twist1 in the perimysial population by Runx2 is necessary to maintain the expression level of perimysial marker gene Aldh1a2, which may be important for regulating muscle development.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the rescue of Aldh1a2 expression and muscle defects in Osr2-Cre;Runx2fl/fl;Twist1fl/+ mice (Figure 6J-L, Figure 6B-G).

claim: The regulation of myogenesis by perimysial CNC-derived cells through Runx2-Twist1 interaction in the soft palate might also be shared by other craniofacial musculoskeletal structures.
source: In summary, our study reveals a complex cellular heterogeneity within the developing soft palate and demonstrates that distinct subpopulations of CNC-derived cells are associated with distinct functions, which coordinate to form intricately connected components of the oropharyngeal complex. Moreover, the regulation of myogenesis by perimysial CNC-derived cells through Runx2-Twist1 interaction in the soft palate might also be shared by other craniofacial musculoskeletal structures.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression of perimysial markers in multiple craniofacial muscle regions (Figure 1P-R, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-E).
